 Smith wary of ‘enormous’ cost of student loan reform
 Fearing that redrawing the system could force cuts on the further education sector, skills minister suggests it is unlikely to happen anytime soon
 Published on 
 November 18, 2026 
 Last updated 
 November 18, 2026 
 Jack Grove Twitter: @jgro_the 
 Share on bluesky 
 Share on linkedin 
 Share on twitter 
 Share on facebook 
 Share on mail 
 Source: UK Government 
 Skills minister Jacqui Smith has appeared to rule out significant reform of student finance arrangements in England, stating it would “cost an enormous amount of money” from the overall skills budget.
 Speaking at the annual conference of Independent Higher Education, which represents private and specialised providers, Smith said it was unrealistic to expect the Westminster government to make major changes regarding how undergraduates repay their tuition or maintenance loans.
 “If we want major reform of student finance, let no-one be under any illusions that it will cost a minimal amount of money,” said Smith whose brief as covers both higher and further education.
 “If we want to reform student finance, we have to think fundamentally about how we spend enormous amounts of money subsidising people into higher education, which is then taken away from other parts of the skills sector,” she continued, adding: “Essentially, that’s part of my concern about it.”
 ADVERTISEMENT 
 Smith’s apparent decision to rule out wider reform of student loans comes despite Lucy Powell stating the issue was at the “top of my in-tray” when starting as education secretary in July. As Labour’s deputy leader under Keir Starmer, Powell said the interest rates paid by graduates on Plan 2 loans (issued between 2012-13 and 2022-23) were “egregious” and that she wanted to “make sure we look at this so it’s fair for students”.
 On whether the system would be reformed, Smith told the audience on 18 November that the issue had become “much more of a concern” but it mattered “more to graduates than it [does] to those accessing higher education”.
 ADVERTISEMENT 
 “There’s still no evidence that people aren’t wanting to go into higher education, and they are taking up student finance Plan 5 now, not Plan 2, which is where most of the focus and concern for graduates has been,” she said.
 The government had taken “some action to try to give a bit more certainty in Plan 2 on interest rates by capping interest rates,” said Smith on the move to ensure rates do not go above 6 per cent from September 2026.
 However, while major reform of student finance “may be something down the track”, said Smith, “this isn’t going to cost a minimal amount of money”.
 “Frankly, there are set priorities here, and I think there are different ways to support people who are finding challenges in their cost of living linked to repayments of student loans – and those are things that we’re doing – like free childcare, housing access, a whole range of other help with bills, a whole range of things to help people with those costs,” said Smith.
 ADVERTISEMENT 
 Addressing concerns about the withdrawal of apprenticeship funding for over-25 – as proposed by Alan Milburn’s review on youth unemployment – Smith said she agreed resources should be refocused on young learners.
 “I have made the case that the shift towards younger people is the key priority of government [which would] address the 40 per cent fall in apprenticeship starts [for under-25s] since 2014-15,” said Smith.
 That did not mean, however, that degree apprenticeships would be sidelined despite most of these being taken by older learners, she continued.
 “The prime minister is often banging on about them and the message has got through that he is very keen on degree apprenticeships,” said Smith.
